title: A Scorebook and a Diamond Plan
bigQuestion: Why does baseball keep a paper book beside the field?

story.title: Ink Beside the Bags
story.kicker: A scorebook lies open on a bench while the diamond waits empty.
paragraphs: The bags are in the dirt. A paper book sits on the bench. Someone will write names and outs in that book when the game begins. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
Henry Chadwick helped make the box score a public habit in the nineteenth century. The book turned a day on the field into a record other towns could read.

A diamond plan is the other paper: a measured drawing of ninety feet. Together the plan and the book are the institution, not a secret code. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
This chapter names the scorebook, the box score, and the plan. It still does not teach a swing. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
story.think: What can a book remember that the dirt will forget?

lessons.title: The Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: A box score is a table of names and numbers that tells what happened in a game.
reading: A box score is a printed table. It lists players and counts such as runs and hits. A reader who was not at the field can still see the outline of the day.
Newspapers in the nineteenth century printed box scores so distant fans could follow clubs on the road.
The box score is not a playbook. It does not show a swing. It shows a record.

words.d: a table of names and counts from one baseball game
a written memory of what happened

lessons.title: Henry Chadwick
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick helped make the baseball box score a public habit.
reading: Henry Chadwick was a writer in New York. He reported baseball and pushed for clear printed records.
People call him a father of baseball writing. He did not invent the diamond. He helped invent how the public read the diamond.
His work belongs with paper, not with coaching. The scorebook on the bench is in that family.

lessons.title: The Scorebook on the Bench
lessons.mainIdea: A scorebook is the notebook a team or official uses to write the game as it happens.
reading: A scorebook is a paper notebook with grids. Someone sits and marks outs, runs, and who batted.
After the game the book can feed a box score. The dirt will be raked. The book remains.
School teams still keep books. The habit is older than any living player on a current roster.

lessons.title: Drawing Ninety Feet
lessons.mainIdea: A diamond plan is a measured drawing of the field, including ninety feet between bases.
reading: A plan shows first, second, third, and home. It marks ninety feet. It is a map, not a photograph of a swing.
Groundskeepers and school crews use plans so two fields can match well enough to host the same rule book.
In this course, pencil art of a diamond should be a plan plus objects, not a player mid-swing.

lessons.title: Paper Travels With the Club
lessons.mainIdea: Clubs on the road in the 1800s needed the next town to mark the same diamond.
reading: A traveling club in the 1860s carried bats and a rule sense of ninety feet. If the next lot was wrong, the race changed.
The 1869 Red Stockings could tour because towns already understood a diamond. The paper made the lot a room.
That is the same lesson as soccer's Laws: the words have to arrive with the people.

lessons.title: Illinois School Paper
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA baseball uses school scorebooks and school diamonds on a state series that began crowning champions in 1940.
reading: An Illinois school game still produces a book. The IHSA series, with a first champion in 1940, needs those records.
The association does not own every diamond. It owns the series rules. Districts own the ground.
1940 is not 1845. One date is a New York club. The other is an Illinois school meet.

lessons.title: The Official Scorer
lessons.mainIdea: A baseball game names an official scorer who writes the official record.
reading: Leagues appoint an official scorer. That person decides how to write hits, errors, and runs in the official report.
The scorer is not the umpire. The umpire calls balls and strikes. The scorer writes the table that becomes the box score.
Henry Chadwick's public tables needed someone in the park whose writing counted as the official memory.

words.d: the person whose written record is the official account of the game

lessons.title: Who Is Missing From Early Books
lessons.mainIdea: Early box scores mostly named men on club rosters that shut many people out.
reading: A box score looks complete. It is only complete for the people who were allowed to play that day.
Women, and later Black players locked out by a league color line, will have their own chapters. Grade 3 starts with the fact that a table can hide an absence.
Asking who is not on the list is a history question. It is not a slogan.

lessons.title: The Catcher's Mask
lessons.mainIdea: A catcher's mask came into baseball in the 1870s as new equipment, not as a play.
reading: In the 1870s catchers began to wear a face mask. Writers often credit a Harvard catcher, James Tyng, with using an early mask in 1877.
The mask is equipment on a face. It changed who could stand close behind the batter as pitching got faster.
Naming the mask is history of gear. It is not a lesson in how to catch.
